--- title: "Estimating EIR from prevalence" --- A parasite survey gives a prevalence, the transmission model needs an EIR, and estiMINT inverts the one into the other with six covariates describing the setting going in alongside it. Prevalence alone is not enough. ## The prevalence model The model ships inside the installed package, so `load_xgb_model` takes its name rather than a path. The call is offline. ::: {#fac728d0 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import pandas as pd from estimint import load_xgb_model, run_xgb_model prev_model = load_xgb_model("prevalence") prev_model["features"] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` ['dn0_use', 'Q0', 'phi_bednets', 'seasonal', 'itn_use', 'irs_use', 'prev_y9'] ``` ::: ::: All seven columns are required. | Column | Meaning | |---|---| | `dn0_use` | Probability a mosquito dies on contact with a net. From `calculate_dn0`. | | `Q0` | Human blood index, 0 to 1 | | `phi_bednets` | Share of bites taken while people are in bed | | `seasonal` | 0 perennial, 1 strongly seasonal | | `itn_use` | ITN coverage, 0 to 1. From `calculate_dn0`. | | `irs_use` | IRS coverage, 0 to 1 | | `prev_y9` | Parasite prevalence in the deployment year, 0 to 1 | `run_xgb_model` takes the frame and the model and returns a NumPy array with one element per row, raising a `ValueError` that names any missing column, though `prevalence` is accepted as an alias for `prev_y9` and copied across. `estimate_eir_with_mosquito_delta` expects that name too. ::: {#2b05cf05 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} setting = dict( dn0_use=0.33, Q0=0.87, phi_bednets=0.82, seasonal=0.0, itn_use=0.6, irs_use=0.0, ) one = pd.DataFrame([{**setting, "prevalence": 0.30}]) eir = run_xgb_model(one, prev_model) type(eir), eir ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` (numpy.ndarray, array([13.39696895])) ``` ::: ::: A prevalence of 30% here implies 13.4 infectious bites per person per year. ## Sweeping prevalence Sweeping the prevalence with the setting held fixed shows an EIR nowhere near linear in it. ::: {#80757df5 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} sweep = pd.DataFrame( [{**setting, "prevalence": p} for p in [0.05, 0.10, 0.20, 0.30, 0.45, 0.60, 0.75]] ) sweep["eir"] = run_xgb_model(sweep, prev_model) sweep[["prevalence", "eir"]].round(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ```{=html}
prevalence eir
0 0.05 1.47
1 0.10 2.87
2 0.20 6.79
3 0.30 13.40
4 0.45 28.82
5 0.60 64.22
6 0.75 158.88
``` ::: ::: ::: {#9eb8367b .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np grid = pd.DataFrame([{**setting, "prevalence": p} for p in np.linspace(0.05, 0.75, 71)]) grid["eir"] = run_xgb_model(grid, prev_model) fig, ax = plt.subplots() ax.plot(grid["prevalence"], grid["eir"], color="#00d4aa") ax.set_xlabel("Prevalence") ax.set_ylabel("EIR (infectious bites per person per year)") plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Inferred EIR against prevalence, holding the setting fixed.](estimating-eir_files/figure-html/cell-6-output-1.png){fig-alt='A teal line rising slowly from near zero at 5% prevalence then climbing very steeply above 60% prevalence, reaching about 160 infectious bites per person per year at 75%.'} ::: ::: The teal curve is nearly flat below a prevalence of 0.3 and climbs almost vertically above 0.6. Prevalence saturates while transmission does not, so once most of the population carries parasites, a further rise in prevalence can only come from a very large rise in the bites behind it. An input a few points out at 70% therefore moves the inferred EIR by tens of bites per year. The same error at 20% moves it by less than one. ## The role of the setting The same measured prevalence implies different EIRs in different settings. Net coverage is the covariate that moves the answer most. Only the coverage varies below. ::: {#61b4ee64 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} from estimint import calculate_dn0 rows = [] for coverage in [0.0, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9]: nets = calculate_dn0(0.30, py_only=coverage) rows.append({ "coverage": coverage, "dn0_use": nets.dn0, "itn_use": nets.itn_use, "Q0": 0.85, "phi_bednets": 0.80, "seasonal": 0.0, "irs_use": 0.0, "prevalence": 0.45, }) nets_vs_eir = pd.DataFrame(rows) nets_vs_eir["eir"] = run_xgb_model(nets_vs_eir, prev_model) nets_vs_eir[["coverage", "dn0_use", "itn_use", "prevalence", "eir"]].round(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ```{=html}
coverage dn0_use itn_use prevalence eir
0 0.0 0.000 0.0 0.45 22.536
1 0.3 0.311 0.3 0.45 24.170
2 0.5 0.311 0.5 0.45 26.461
3 0.7 0.311 0.7 0.45 31.960
4 0.9 0.311 0.9 0.45 37.058
``` ::: ::: Every row reports the same prevalence, and the inferred EIR still rises by roughly two thirds down the column, because a district that holds 45% prevalence under 90% net coverage must be absorbing far more infectious bites than one that holds it with no nets. Understating `itn_use` therefore biases the EIR downwards. Please see [Nets and dn0](nets-and-dn0.qmd) for that error. `irs_use` acts the same way and far more strongly. ::: {#f65abc2a .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} irs = pd.DataFrame( [{"dn0_use": 0.40, "Q0": 0.85, "phi_bednets": 0.80, "seasonal": 0.0, "itn_use": 0.50, "irs_use": v, "prevalence": 0.30} for v in [0.0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8]] ) irs["eir"] = run_xgb_model(irs, prev_model) irs[["irs_use", "prevalence", "eir"]].round(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7} ```{=html}
irs_use prevalence eir
0 0.0 0.3 12.13
1 0.2 0.3 25.34
2 0.4 0.3 47.53
3 0.6 0.3 104.70
4 0.8 0.3 204.43
``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-warning} ## High IRS inflates the estimated EIR Holding prevalence fixed, the inferred EIR climbs steeply with `irs_use`, from about 12 with no spraying to about 200 at 80% coverage. Indoor spraying suppresses transmission hard, so a setting that still shows 30% prevalence under heavy IRS is read as one with a very high underlying EIR. The estimate is only as good as the `irs_use` you supply, and a value that is too high, or a scenario that pairs a high prevalence with heavy spraying, pushes the EIR into the top of the training range or past it, where it is then clamped. Check the estimated EIR before trusting a trajectory built on it. ::: ## The global model `set_global_model` registers a model as the default, after which `run_xgb_model` may be called with the frame alone, and `get_global_model` returns whatever is currently registered. ::: {#815555d1 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} from estimint import set_global_model, get_global_model set_global_model(prev_model) run_xgb_model(one) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=8} ``` array([13.39696895]) ``` ::: ::: ::: {#3ff4cad8 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} get_global_model()["class"] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=9} ``` 'estiMINT_model' ``` ::: ::: Note that the global slot holds exactly one model, so pass the model explicitly in any script that touches more than one of the three, because a stray `set_global_model` elsewhere changes what an unqualified call resolves to. ::: {.callout-note} ## The valid range `prev_y9` is clamped to `[0.005, 0.80]`, and values outside that band are pulled to the nearest edge. No warning is raised. ::: {#93198e2b .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} edges = pd.DataFrame( [{**setting, "prevalence": p} for p in [0.001, 0.005, 0.80, 0.95]] ) edges["eir"] = run_xgb_model(edges, prev_model) edges[["prevalence", "eir"]].round(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=10} ```{=html}
prevalence eir
0 0.001 0.894
1 0.005 0.894
2 0.800 234.882
3 0.950 234.882
``` ::: ::: A sweep producing an implausibly flat EIR at either end has almost always hit this clamp. ::: ## See also Please see [EIR and HBR](eir-and-hbr.qmd) for the same inversion run from entomological data in both directions, and [Mosquito density and EIR](mosquito-density.qmd) for the EIR when the vector population changes.
